# Cruise Liner Sinks After Striking Iceberg in Antarctic Waters

LONDON, England (CNN) -- More than 150 people have been forced to abandon a sinking cruise liner following a collision with an iceberg in Antarctic waters, a Chilean navy captain confirmed to CNN. The vessel issued a distress call at approximately 10 p.m. ET on Thursday.

The passenger ship *Explorer* reported difficulties near the South Shetland Islands, south of Argentina—a region within the sector of Antarctica claimed by the United Kingdom. Capt. Carlos Munita of the Chilean navy stated that authorities received the distress signal from the *Explorer* around 10 p.m. ET Thursday, after the ship struck an iceberg. He further noted that a Norwegian rescue vessel had since arrived at the scene.

According to tour operators, the *Explorer* is a passenger ship that operates voyages between South America and Antarctica. The vessel, which sails under a Liberian flag, was reportedly carrying 154 people on board, including 100 passengers. The nationalities of those aboard have not yet been disclosed.

Passengers and crew were evacuated into lifeboats, though the captain and first officer are reported to have remained aboard the ship.

"The great majority of people, including all the passengers, have been safely taken off the *Explorer* and are now being recovered by the first of the vessels to arrive on the scene in response to the distress call," said Dave Jardine-Smith, head of the Maritime and Coastguard Agency's (MCA) search and rescue team in England.

"The passengers and crew from the *Explorer* have not been in the lifeboats very long," he added. "They should, hopefully, be in good condition. We are told there are no injuries."

Earlier, Mark Clark, a spokesman for the MCA, told the Press Association that five ships were en route to assist the stricken vessel. "She hit something and is taking on a serious amount of water—that is all we know," he said.

Forecasters told the Press Association that air temperatures in the area hovered around minus 5°C, with sea temperatures near minus 1°C. Stephen Davenport, senior forecaster with MeteoGroup, warned of the dangers posed by such conditions: "It wouldn't take long for hypothermia to set in at that kind of temperature in the sea. They do get very bad storms down that way, and gale-force winds especially, because there is no land in the way to offer protection."

Lt. Matt Alex of the U.S. Coast Guard Atlantic Area command center confirmed that the vessel is owned by Gap Adventures, a company based in Toronto, Canada.

**LONDON, England (CNN)** -- According to a Chilean naval officer who spoke with CNN, upwards of 150 individuals evacuated a cruise ship that began taking on water after striking an iceberg in the waters off Antarctica. The stricken vessel radioed for emergency assistance late Thursday night, around 10 p.m. ET.

The Explorer, a passenger cruise ship, ran into trouble close to the South Shetland Islands, positioned south of Argentina—a region of Antarctic territory that Britain lays claim to.

Chilean navy Captain Carlos Munita confirmed his team picked up the emergency transmission from the Explorer, which indicated the ship had struck an iceberg at approximately 10 p.m. Thursday (Eastern time). He noted that a rescue vessel from Norway had already reached the location.

According to tour operators, the Explorer typically ferries travelers on excursions connecting South America with Antarctic destinations. Reports indicate 154 individuals were aboard the Liberian-flagged ship, roughly 100 of them passengers—though their countries of origin remain unconfirmed.

While passengers and crew members made their way into lifeboats during the evacuation, both the ship's captain and first officer reportedly chose to remain aboard.

Dave Jardine-Smith, who heads search and rescue operations for England's Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA), stated: "The great majority of people, including all the passengers, have been safely taken off the Explorer and are now being recovered by the first of the vessels to arrive on scene in response to the distress call."

# Cruise Ship Strikes Iceberg Near Antarctica; All 342 Passengers Safely Evacuated

**By CNN Staff**

*(CNN)* — A cruise ship carrying more than 340 passengers and crew struck an iceberg in the frigid waters near the Antarctic Peninsula early Tuesday, forcing an emergency evacuation that maritime officials are calling a "textbook execution" of safety protocols under extreme conditions.

The vessel, the *Polar Horizon*, operated by Arctic & Antarctic Expeditions Ltd., was on a two-week sightseeing voyage through the Drake Passage when it collided with a submerged ice formation around 4:15 a.m. local time, according to the company and the Chilean Maritime Authority, which coordinated rescue efforts.

The impact tore a gash in the ship's starboard hull below the waterline, triggering flooding in several lower compartments. Crew members activated emergency protocols within minutes, sounding the ship's general alarm and directing passengers to muster stations.

"We felt a violent shudder, like the whole ship had hit a wall," said passenger Diane Whitfield, 61, of Toronto, speaking by satellite phone from a rescue vessel. "Then the alarms went off, and the crew was incredibly calm. They had us in our life jackets and moving toward the lifeboats within 15 minutes."

All 342 people aboard — 268 passengers and 74 crew — were evacuated into a fleet of lifeboats and inflatable rafts within roughly 90 minutes, according to the cruise line. The evacuation was completed before sunrise, in near-freezing temperatures and choppy seas, though officials say the absence of high winds was a critical factor in preventing casualties.

"This could have been a catastrophe," said Capt. Elena Vasquez of the Chilean Navy, which dispatched two icebreakers and a helicopter unit to the scene. "The crew's training and the passengers' cooperation made the difference between a difficult night and a tragedy."

Nearby vessels, including a Norwegian research ship and an Argentine naval icebreaker, responded to distress calls and began picking up survivors from the water and lifeboats within hours. No deaths have been reported. Officials said a small number of passengers were treated for hypothermia and minor injuries aboard rescue ships, but none of the injuries were described as life-threatening.

The *Polar Horizon* remained partially afloat but listing several hours after the collision, according to satellite imagery reviewed by maritime analysts. Salvage teams were expected to assess the vessel once weather conditions stabilized, though officials cautioned it may ultimately be declared a total loss.

The International Association of Antarctica Tour Operators (IAATO) said it would be conducting a full investigation into the incident, along with Chilean and flag-state authorities. Questions are expected to focus on the ship's navigation systems, ice-detection radar, and whether the vessel was operating within recommended safety corridors given current ice conditions in the region.

Antarctic tourism has grown rapidly in the past decade, with tens of thousands of travelers now visiting the continent each year aboard expedition-style cruise ships. Experts have long warned that increased shipping traffic in remote polar waters raises the risk of ice-related incidents, given the difficulty of rescue operations in such isolated conditions.

"This is a wake-up call for the entire industry," said Mark Delaney, a maritime safety consultant not affiliated with the cruise line. "You're operating thousands of miles from major rescue infrastructure. When something goes wrong down there, you're relying almost entirely on other ships in the area and a lot of luck with the weather."

The cruise line said in a statement that it was "immensely grateful" for the safety of all those aboard and pledged full cooperation with investigators. "The well-being of our guests and crew is our top priority," the statement read. "We are working closely with authorities to understand what happened and to support everyone affected."

Survivors were expected to be transported to Ushuaia, Argentina, the southernmost city in the world and a common departure point for Antarctic cruises, within the next two days.

This story is developing and will be updated.

# Liberian-Flagged Cruise Ship Sinks After Iceberg Collision; Rescue Operation Underway in North Atlantic

**By CNN Staff**

A Liberian-flagged passenger vessel carrying more than 900 people sank in the North Atlantic early Tuesday after striking an iceberg, triggering a massive multinational rescue operation in treacherous winter conditions, maritime officials said.

The vessel, identified as the MV *Nordic Star*, was en route from Southampton, England, to Halifax, Nova Scotia, when it collided with the iceberg shortly before 2 a.m. local time approximately 400 nautical miles southeast of Newfoundland, according to the ship's operator, Crestline Maritime.

The company said the vessel sustained a significant breach to its hull and began taking on water rapidly. The captain issued a distress call within minutes, and the crew initiated evacuation procedures, deploying lifeboats and life rafts as passengers were roused from their cabins.

"The situation deteriorated very quickly," said Erik Halvorsen, a spokesperson for Crestline Maritime, in a statement to CNN. "Our crew followed emergency protocols, but conditions on the water made this an extraordinarily difficult rescue."

## Harsh Weather Complicates Response

The US Coast Guard, working alongside Canadian search-and-rescue teams and vessels diverted from nearby shipping lanes, said the rescue effort was hampered by rough seas, sub-zero temperatures and limited visibility.

Waves were reported at 12 to 15 feet, with air temperatures hovering around 14 degrees Fahrenheit (-10 Celsius) and water temperatures near freezing — conditions that officials say leave survivors in the water only minutes before hypothermia becomes life-threatening.

"This is about as challenging an environment as you can face," said Coast Guard Rear Adm. Karen Ellison during a briefing Tuesday afternoon. "Every hour matters in these temperatures."

Three commercial vessels responded to the distress call, alongside Canadian Forces aircraft that dropped flares and rescue equipment to illuminate the area and assist those in lifeboats. A Canadian Cormorant helicopter squadron based in Gander, Newfoundland, was also dispatched.

## Passengers Rescued, Some Unaccounted For

As of Tuesday evening, officials said at least 780 passengers and crew had been rescued and transported to nearby vessels or airlifted to shore facilities in Newfoundland. Search efforts were continuing for others believed to still be missing, though officials cautioned that numbers remained fluid as rescue teams worked through the night.

Survivors described chaotic scenes as the ship listed sharply before going under roughly three hours after impact.

"We heard this enormous grinding noise, and then the alarms started," said passenger Marta Jensen, who was reached by phone after being brought aboard a cargo ship that assisted in the rescue. "People were calm at first, but once we saw the deck tilting, it was terrifying."

## Investigation to Follow

The *Nordic Star*, built in 2011 and registered in Monrovia, Liberia, had a capacity of just over 1,000 passengers and crew. Maritime authorities said the vessel's flag state, along with international maritime bodies, would investigate the circumstances of the collision, including questions about ice warnings issued in the region in recent days.

The International Ice Patrol had flagged increased iceberg activity along the shipping corridor in a bulletin issued last week, a routine advisory during winter months in the North Atlantic.

This incident echoes the region's grim maritime history — the area lies not far from where the *Titanic* sank after striking an iceberg in 1912 — though officials stressed that modern satellite tracking, radar and safety protocols significantly reduce such risks today.

Crestline Maritime said it was setting up a family assistance hotline and would provide updates as the search-and-rescue operation continued. Canadian and U.S. authorities said they did not expect to scale back efforts before Wednesday, citing the ongoing search for missing individuals.

CNN's maritime and weather teams are continuing to follow this developing story.
